extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply precise conceptual distinctions about causation and the composition of causes that underpin a rigorous canon of induction (what counts as a cause, necessity/unconditionality, agent vs patient, composition and permanence of causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as unconditional antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a phenomenon is the antecedent, or the concurrence of antecedents, upon which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that 'invariable sequence' alone is insufficient; the antecedent must be such that, so long as the present constitution of things endures (i.e., absent changes in relevant conditions), the consequent will always follow. The text offers the day/night example to show sequences that are invariable historically but conditional, and proposes the alternative phrasing for 'cause' as 'assemblage of positive conditions, subject to no other than negative conditions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish unconditional causation from conditional uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Invariable succession (uniformity in past experience) is not synonymous with causation unless the sequence is unconditional — that is, not dependent on additional antecedents whose presence is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: day and night are uniformly successive but conditional (depend on sun rising) and therefore not causes of each other; Earth's orbital series is invariable in experience but conditional on coexistence of specific forces. The practical task of induction includes ascertaining whether an apparently invariable antecedent is truly a condition or merely accompanies the true conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive conditions vs negative conditions in cause statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving a complete expression of a cause, include all positive conditions; negative conditions (i.e., absence of counteracting agencies) may be regarded as implicitly contained in the positive laws of other agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid listing negative conditions separately when they are better regarded as implicit in positive laws of other agents. Example: listing every counteracting agency is impractical; better to include positive conditions and treat negatives as implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent and patient are not fundamentally distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The common distinction between agent (that which acts) and patient (that which is acted on) is largely a verbal or logical fiction rather than a fundamental metaphysical distinction; what we call 'states of objects' are often themselves phenomena of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a stone may be called patient when falling, yet can be conceived as agent if asking 'what causes vertical motion toward the earth?'; sensations (prussic acid causing death) involve both agent and active organic properties of the patient. Hence treat 'agent' and 'patient' language cautiously and avoid assuming ontological priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity/conditionalness as central to causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of cause involves the idea of necessity in the sense of unconditionalness — that which will be followed by the consequent under any supposition about other things (i.e., not merely in past experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that 'necessary' here does not mean metaphysical fatalism but that given the relevant conditions (and absence of counteracting ones) the consequent must follow. This differentiates causal laws from mere observed conjunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal relation: cause need not be perceptibly prior
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause does not necessarily precede its effect by a perceptible interval; cause and effect may coincide or be simultaneous, though the effect never precedes the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While precedence can help determine direction when two coexistent phenomena are compared, microscopic or imperceptible intermediates may fill apparent simultaneity. The practical definition of causation (law of succession) is not undermined by possible simultaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production vs continuance: some effects require continuous causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate conditions necessary for the initial production of a phenomenon from those required for its continuance; some phenomena are instantaneous and must be perpetually reproduced by their cause, others persist without continued presence of the producing agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: illumination is instantaneous and must be renewed as long as conditions subsist; a ploughshare continues to exist after forging without continuous heating. Use this distinction to avoid the mistaken axiom that the continued existence of a cause is always required to sustain its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes and intermixture of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple agents act jointly, the joint effect can sometimes be predicted deductively from the separate effects, provided the same laws that express each single-agent effect correctly express the part due to that agent in the combined effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition (that individual laws also correctly express contributory parts) is realized in many important cases and underlies deductive composition of causes. Where it fails, joint effects may be novel and require empirical investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: One cause may produce heterogeneous effects (properties/powers language)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single phenomenon (agent) can be followed by several heterogeneous effects; we name these different effects as arising from different properties or powers of the cause (gravitative, luminiferous, calorific, magnetic, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'properties and powers' phrasing is a convenient abbrevation for denoting connections between causes and diverse effects; it is an instrument of thought and abridgment rather than an explanatory mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent causes (primeval causes) and limits of explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist permanent natural agents (sun, earth, elements) whose continued existence and properties account for many phenomena; the origin or ultimate distribution of these primeval causes is not scientifically explicable and cannot be reduced to laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences dependent on the casual coexistence of primeval causes are not classified as universal laws of nature; predictions involving them require direct evidence of the requisite distribution of agents in space.

rubrics_metrics.name: All non-primeval phenomena are effects traceable to antecedent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for primeval causes, everything that begins to exist is an effect immediate or remote of earlier phenomena; the state of the universe at any instant is the consequence of its previous state given the agents, collocation, and laws of agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, perfect knowledge of all agents and their properties would permit construction of the universe's subsequent history (barring external volition). This supports a deterministic schema for scientific prediction though practical computation is infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistences among effects are reducible to laws of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable coexistences between effects cannot constitute independent unconditional laws distinct from laws of causation; such uniformities arise because of identity or coexistence of their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only unconditional coexistences sufficiently invariable to be laws are those between different independent effects of the same cause (i.e., different properties of one agent)—the topic later treated as Specific Properties of Kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve 'cause' terminology to mark a key distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if 'efficient' or metaphysical causes are inaccessible (Comte's point), retaining the term 'cause' is valuable to distinguish relations of unconditional succession (laws of causation) from other constant relations of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author agrees with Comte that ultimate efficient causes are beyond human access but argues that the term 'cause' aptly designates the class of relations (unconditional succession) important for framing a rigorous canon of induction; avoiding the word may obscure this distinction.
